blocks.text: Xerox Art, also called Copy Art, Electrostatic Art, or Xerography, is a photomechanical art form built around the office photocopier rather than a camera or a printing press. Prints are made by pressing objects, photographs, or body parts directly onto the glass platen of a machine and pressing "start," a process that yields sharp, one-to-one reproductions where the object touches the glass and increasingly distorted, ghostly renderings the further it strays from the surface. Because the photocopier was engineered for the reproduction of flat office documents rather than for artistic use, its mechanical quirks, the fixed shallow depth of field, the halogen lamp's narrow throw of light, and the toner's tendency to degrade with each successive copy, became the raw material of the aesthetic itself.

The technical foundation of the aesthetic predates its adoption by artists by more than two decades. The first electrophotographic image, marked "10-22-38 Astoria," was produced by inventor Chester Carlson and his assistant Otto Kornei in a rented Queens apartment using static electricity generated by rubbing a handkerchief against a sulfur-coated plate. Carlson spent the next two decades refining the process, and the Xerox Haloid company's first fully automated plain-paper copier, the Xerox 914, reached the office market in 1959. Unlike the wet Thermofax process, which required proprietary heat-sensitive paper, the 914 could copy onto ordinary bond paper, a distinction that would later make the photocopier cheap and accessible enough for artists to adopt.

Artists began experimenting with the machines almost as soon as they appeared. Charles Arnold, Jr., an instructor at the Rochester Institute of Technology, is credited with making the first photocopies with explicit artistic intent in 1961, while Wallace Berman, regarded as a father of assemblage art, arranged Verifax copies into grid-like juxtapositions influenced by his San Francisco Beat circle, Surrealism, and the Kabbalah. Esta Nesbitt developed three named xerography techniques during her research partnership with Xerox Corporation between 1970 and 1972, and Sonia Landy Sheridan began teaching the first academic course on the artistic use of copiers at the Art Institute of Chicago in 1970. Seth Siegelaub and Jack Wendler's 1968 Untitled (Xerox Book), made with seven conceptual artists including Carl Andre, Sol LeWitt, and Robert Morris, treated the copier as a conceptual tool rather than a means of imitation; in the same year, Alighiero Boetti photocopied his own face and hand while signing his wife's name in Nove Xerox AnneMarie, exploiting a machine that, as curator Michelle Cotton observed, "can see but can't hear."

Two cities recur throughout the history of the form: Rochester, home to Eastman Kodak and Xerox and known as the Imaging Capital of the World, and San Francisco, where a proliferation of copy shops through the 1970s gave artists cheap and repeated access to the machines. That city's scene took organized form with the 1976 All Xerox exhibition at the LaMamelle gallery and the 1980 International Copy Art Exhibition, curated by Ginny Lloyd, which later traveled to San Jose and Japan. Louise Odes Neaderland founded the International Society of Copier Artists in 1981 to publish collaborative mail art and artist books in small xerographic editions, and its quarterly became a venue for artists such as Rebecca Stuckey, who captioned domestic interiors with disquieting titles like "radiation" and "darkens," unsettling the familiarity of the images. Writing in the same publication, art librarian Judith Hoffberg framed the form's accessibility in explicitly democratic terms, paraphrasing Marshall McLuhan's remark that where Gutenberg had made all men readers, xerography had made all men publishers.

Institutional recognition followed through the 1980s. Marilyn McCray curated Electroworks at the Cooper-Hewitt Museum and the International Museum of Photography at George Eastman House in 1980, showing more than 250 prints, books, and three-dimensional pieces, and the 1987 Stuttgart exhibition "Medium: Photocopie" was accompanied by a catalogue documenting new approaches to the medium. Marking the 75th anniversary of Carlson's first photocopy, curator Michelle Cotton's 2013 exhibition "Xerography" at firstsite in Colchester brought together more than 125 works by 39 artists, from Josh Smith's wallpaper installations to Jenny Holzer's redacted intelligence documents, and was accompanied by an on-site copy shop that printed the catalogue on demand. More recently, the Whitney Museum presented Experiments in Electrostatics: Photocopy Art from the Whitney's Collection, 1966-1986, organized by curatorial fellow Michelle Donnelly, closing in March of 2018.

The gendered history of the office copier shaped much of this recognition. As industrialization expanded the volume of clerical reproduction demanded of offices in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, women were channeled into copying, transcription, and shorthand work, but excluded from roles regarded as requiring invention; critics extended the same logic to women artists, whose work was often dismissed as derivative even as their male peers' "gesture" was celebrated in movements such as abstract expressionism. Copier art, made largely through organizations like the International Society of Copier Artists with a majority-women membership, has since been read as a challenge to that creator-copyist binary, reframing the act of reproduction itself as a legitimate site of originality.

Xerox Art is defined less by a fixed palette than by the physical limitations of the machine it is produced on. Because the photocopier was built to hold sharp focus only on a flat document pressed to the glass, its depth of field is fixed and deliberately shallow; when a rounded or sculptural object is copied, only the surface in direct contact with the platen resolves clearly, while the rest of the form dissolves into blur, giving the image the compressed, cropped quality seen in Pati Hill's Alphabet of Common Objects. This shallow focus combines with the machine's naturally high contrast, tuned by manufacturers to preserve the legibility of typed text, to produce stark, charcoal-like blacks and blown-out whites; some artists intensified this quality further; Hill, for instance, deliberately overfilled her IBM Copier II's toner cartridge to obtain richer blacks reminiscent of etching and charcoal drawing.

The perspective of the copied image is itself unusual: because the object rests against the glass, the resulting print shows "the side of your subject that you do not see," in Hill's words, an underside view weighted by the pull of gravity that gives copied objects and bodies a pressed, almost embalmed quality. Self-portraiture exploits this directly, as in Barbara T. Smith's 1976 Artist in the Science Lab, where her face and hand are flattened against the platen, or Andy Warhol's 1969 self-portrait, whose owner reportedly found the resulting image "morbid" enough to keep off the apartment wall. Movement during the scan, whether of a hand pulled away from the glass mid-copy or of small objects like marbles rolled across the platen, produces stretched, doubled, or smeared forms, a technique sometimes called Image Decomposition or Copy Motion.

A further recurring technique is Degeneration: photocopying a copy of a copy, again and again, so that each successive generation loses fidelity to the source. Robert Morris applied this to a photograph of Earth for the 1968 Xerox Book, so that the planet's clouds gained dark, gritty drop-shadowed edges as its surface faded into abstraction, and in 1985 Timm Ulrich recopied the title of Walter Benjamin's essay on mechanical reproduction one hundred times until the text dissolved into illegible graphic noise. Rather than treating this loss of fidelity as a flaw to correct, many copier artists treated it, along with incidental toner speckling and streaking, as a source of texture in its own right. Other established approaches include Direct Imaging, the straightforward copying of items placed on the platen; Still Life Collage, in which multiple objects are arranged into a foreground-background composition; Overprinting, which builds layered compositions by running the same sheet through the machine repeatedly; and Copy Overlay, which manipulates the colour-separation mechanism of a colour copier. While most historically significant work was produced in black and white, later colour xerography allowed artists like Laurie-Rae Chamberlain to work in saturated, punk-inflected hues by varying exposure and colour balance controls, a technique referred to as Colorizing.

Xerox Art's aesthetic of cheap and high-contrast reproduction overlaps closely with the do-it-yourself ethos of the Punk movement, where the photocopier was used as the primary tool for producing flyers, fanzines, and record inserts on a limited budget. Destroy All Monsters, the Michigan noise and proto-punk group, launched a fanzine through the copier in 1976, a format the "Xerography" exhibition later placed alongside other artists' copier works as part of the same artistic lineage. The same stark contrast, degraded texture, and collage-based layering also appears throughout the cover art, posters, and photocopied inserts associated with the Minimal Wave genre.
